newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Afghan Taleban advance worries ex-Soviet states.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban advance worries ex-Soviet states.

text.p: The former Soviet republics of Central Asia, alarmed by the rise of Moslem fundamentalism, hastily beefed up their border security on Sunday after advances by the radical Islamist Taleban militia in Afghanistan.

Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan fear that the Taleban's capture on Saturday of the main northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif, a former stronghold of opposition chief General Abdual Rashid Dostum, could upset regional stability.
"Uzbekistan's border troops are taking measures to reinforce the (Afghan) border to exclude any provocations," said a statement issued by the foreign ministry in Tashkent.

"Talks with the border service on the Afghan side are underway to preserve calm and provide security for the population on both sides of the border," it said, adding that no border incidents had occurred so far.
The Turkish foreign ministry announced earlier that Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, had arrived in Ankara after fleeing Afghanistan.

A representative of the Russian border guards in Tajikistan told Reuters that more refugees from Afghanistan were arriving in Tajikistan through the checkpoint at Nizhny Pyandzh, 200 km (125 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov held talks with his security advisers late on Saturday and security officials also met on Sunday to discuss ways of maintaining stability.

Russian border troops have also been put on alert in Kyrgyzstan, Russian news agencies said, and Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev chaired an emergency meeting of his government to discuss reinforcing the republic's southern border.

Military and security officials did not so far see any direct military threat but were concerned at a possible influx of refugees and would go to the southern region of Osh on Tuesday to inspect the border, Irar-Tass news agency said.
In Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov warned the Taleban not to violate the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), successor to the Sovet Union.

"(Any infringement) will provoke very tough and effective actions from the CIS side," Interfax news agency quoted Primakov as saying. Moscow issued a statement on Saturday expressing its alarm over events in Afghanistan.

Primakov has made clear that Moscow regards the Taleban as incapable of uniting Afghanistan, arguing that it lacks broad support among the country's many ethnic minorities, who include Tajiks and Uzbeks.
He said Pakistan and the intelligence services of several Western countries could help to put pressure on the Taleban to behave with restraint.

Russia, which is separated from Afghanistan by more than 1,000 km of Kazakhstan territory, has about 20,000 troops in Tajikistan, where they guard the remote, mountainous Afghan border and view themselves as a shield against Islamist fundamentalism.
Rakhmonov said last month that up to a million refugees could pour from Afghanistan into his impoverished country of 5.7 million people if there was fierce fighting there.
Tajik Foreign Minister Talbak Nazarov said in the Iranian capital Tehran that his war-ravaged country could not cope with such an influx, Interfax news agency reported.

"However our republic will not throw these people to the whim of fate and will make a contribution to helping them, though their best hope lies with other countries and with international organisations," Interfax quoted Nazarov as saying.
Rakhmonov's secular government and the united Islamist opposition agreed last year on a ceasefire to end a four-year civil war in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
